comment.value:
This paper presents a library to help practitioners looking to do research in Offline RL in NetHack.  Building on a large-scale dataset presented last years datasets & benchmarks, the authors implement a library that specifically aims to help Offfline RL researchers get up and running with ‘nld_aa’.  This includes adding benchmarked offline RL implementations, wandb runs and new dataloaders for a ‘split up’ dataset.


**Perceived Strengths:**
* The code and implementations appears to be high quality and genuinely of use to those looking to do Offline RL on NetHack. Several important algorithms are implemented, along with dataloaders that are more natural to q-value based methods (eg s,a,r,s’ tuples vs s,a,r tuples).
* The benchmarks appear to be reproducible with wandb traces, and good RLiable estimates.

**Perceived Weaknesses:**

* There is a repeated suggestion that is only a minor amount of novelty in this work.  The data is repackaged from the original, new implementations of old algorithms are presented. The authors respond that that their clean implementations and better reproducibility are easier for researchers looking to get started offline RL. 


**AC View:**

At surface-level the contributions of this work looks minor: repackaging old data; reimplementing cleaner and reproducible benchmark algorithms; writing new dataloaders; and adding more robust evaluations.  However, as pointed out by one reviewer, this is all the unloved work that leads to good datasets and benchmarks, that benefits the community.  However, often such work is done iteratively, contributing to the original open-source repository and helping to improve the software, and it is reasonable to question whether such contributions are worthy of a separate paper and package. In this case I believe there is a distinguishing factor in the specific targeting of the small scale offline RL setting (over the large-scale one presented in the original dataset), most noticed by splitting up and rigorously benchmarking different algorithms on different datasets.  As such I agree with the majority of reviewers and recommend this benchmark for inclusion.

In light of these responses and clarifications, would you consider supporting our paper for publication? If not, could you let us know what's left unanswered in our response? Perhaps we can provide further clarifications while we can, since there is only one day left for the discussion phase. Best regards!

We would like to thank you for your time reviewing our paper results and valuable comments. We will try to address them below.

> Please verify the requirements to install the library. I attempted to install the library but the pip install fails.
> 

Thanks for letting us know! It seems to be a [recent bug](https://github.com/facebookresearch/nle/issues/359) in the original [nle](https://github.com/facebookresearch/nle) package as well as some missing nle dependencies. Thus, we have added a correction to the installation instructions in the README and also verified that everything works correctly on [google colab](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1kGfOivh67vunV_Wj2JwVTTMHrh_F2Nvo?usp=sharing) and locally. 

> Why normalize the scores if the bot is far from ideal behavior?
> 

Good question! There are two reasons for this. The first is that, despite the non-ideal behavior of the bot, we are still far from even surpassing such non-ideal behavior using existing methods, be it imitation or reinforcement learning. We wanted to put an additional emphasis on this, because just the in game score does not give an understanding of how much worse we are than an expert in the dataset. In this we follow the practices that are already used in the offline rl community, for example in D4RL. Over time, if the dataset changes, for example, when we can outperform the bot, the normalization method will change also to take this into account. The second is that, we use [rliable](https://github.com/google-research/rliable), the evaluation toolbox from Agarwal et al. (2021), to report more accurate estimates when the number of random seeds is small and variability is very high. For most metrics to be computed by rliable, the raw scores must be normalized.

> How does the training time scale with different hardware configurations? How does this compare to the distributed Hambro et al. implementation?
> 

The training time consists of time to sample the data and time to update the networks. 

As we pointed out in the publication, our library provides several implementations for data sampling. Scaling here depends on the amount of available memory. If there is enough memory (120 GB max) to load the dataset completely into memory, the time to sample a batched data will be much shorter than in Hambro et al. If there is not enough memory, one can use the memmap implementation, which will take up disk space, but the sampling will be almost as fast as in memory.

Regarding training time, our goal was to provide clear, robust, and minimalistic implementations, and to make sure that all our experiments can be reproduced on a single GPU in a reasonable amount of time. The baseline implementations that our library currently provides do not support distributed learning, so there is almost no benefit from more GPUs for single seed training. However, due to the lack of modularity and [CleanRL](https://github.com/vwxyzjn/cleanrl)-style implementations, practitioners can easily and with low effort add multi-gpu training using standard techniques (e.g. accelerate or deepspeed libraries).

> Are there reasonable hand-defined metrics to use instead for different levels of success?
> 

Yes, they are. Some of them were defined in the original publication that proposed the Nethack environment, such as collecting gold, finding oracle, etc. The community has its own [сhallenges](https://nethackwiki.com/wiki/Unofficial_conduct), such as completing the game with minimum score and others. However, it seems to us that at these early stages of the game, game score correlates well with progression through the game. Of course, we can imagine that more advanced algorithms will be able to exploit such a reward, but right now this is unlikely. Furthermore, game score is being used in an all recent Nethack publications [1, 2, 3] and changing the progression criteria will make it difficult to compare existing methods with each other.

References:

1. Piterbarg, U., Pinto, L., & Fergus, R. (2023). NetHack is Hard to Hack. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.19240*.
2. Mazoure, B., Bruce, J., Precup, D., Fergus, R., & Anand, A. (2023). Accelerating exploration and representation learning with offline pre-training. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2304.00046*.
3. Hambro, E., Mohanty, S., Babaev, D., Byeon, M., Chakraborty, D., Grefenstette, E., ... & Sypetkowski, M. (2022, July). Insights from the neurips 2021 nethack challenge. In *NeurIPS 2021 Competitions and Demonstrations Track* (pp. 41-52). PMLR.

Thank you for the review and for emphasizing our library's strengths. We tried to address the small issues that you pointed out.

> The 3 obstacles mentioned in the abstract are not consistent with those mentioned in Section 2. In the abstract one of them is tool-wise, but in Section 2 it becomes resource-wise.
> 

Thanks! We fixed this in the updated version of the paper, and it should be consistent now.

> It is not clear how the normalized score (e.g., in Figure 1) is computed. Maybe I missed something. Shouldn't the normalized score lie within [0, 1]?
> 

Sorry about this confusion. Indeed, the normalized score should be within [0, 1], but we rescale it to [0, 100] following the common practice from the standard offline reinforcement learning D4RL benchmark. This does not affect the results or interpretation in any way. We clarify this in the updated version of the paper.

We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and concerns. We tried to address them below.

> It would be nice if the author could elaborate more on the problem formulation. For instance, what are the rules of the game, what does each role, race and alignment stand for, what the general goal is and how human/bot can achieve it, what does each game transition tuple stand for, etc.

We acknowledge the importance of understanding the problem formulation and the game mechanics when studying offline RL in Nethack. Given the intricate and vast nature of the game, providing an exhaustive explanation would require considerable space, potentially diverting the focus from our core contributions. For a more in-depth understanding, we refer readers to the [seminal work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.13760) on the Nethack environment and the comprehensive [game wiki](https://nethackwiki.com/wiki/Main_Page). These resources provide an extensive elucidation of the game rules, roles, races, alignments, and transition tuples. We have added these links in an updated version of the paper.

> There are standard deviations for the benchmark results. Why aren’t they included?

If you are referring to the results of the experiments, 95% confidence intervals are reported in the plots instead. In order to understand the effect of standard deviation and variability, the three metrics **Mean**, **IQM** and **Median** are used, as advised in Agarwal et al., 2021.

> What does Optimality Gap in Figure 1a refer to?

Thank you for bringing to our attention the query regarding the "Optimality Gap" in Figure 1a. We noticed a bug during response preparation. It has been fixed now, and the corrected plots have been incorporated into an updated version of the paper.

**Optimality gap** is the amount by which the algorithm fails to meet a minimum normalized score of 1.0 (or 100.0 in our case, as we rescale the normalized score to [0, 100] range). It also has an interpretation of an area above performance profile curve (see orange region [here](https://postimg.cc/PCxByD5g/f06ae45e), image taken from the original Agarwal et al., 2021 paper). In practice, this metric is a robust alternative to the mean, as it is less susceptible to outliers compared to mean scores.

> Since the proposed dataset is comprised of collected game transition of rule-based agent, how can an agent learning on this dataset exceeding the strength of the rule-based agent or even surpassing human players? The author can elaborate it in Section 4 or 6.

The main promise of offline RL methods is to obtain agents that significantly outperform the policies contained in the dataset, while learning on large amounts of suboptimal data. Furthermore, in fact, having such an suboptimal dataset, the preferred choice is to use offline RL rather than imitation learning, as recent works analyzing this have shown [1, 2]. The large dataset and its suboptimality gives us a hint that offline RL methods might work particularly well here. Unfortunately, this is not the case at the moment and the specific reason is an open question. In our paper we currently already talk about these motivations and outcomes in the introduction and also in the results.

> It might be too early to come to a conclusion that BC >= ORL before hyperparameter searching or exploring different algorithmic implementations.

Indeed, to draw strong conclusions on such a difficult environment with a lot of randomness one needs to have data for a lot of random seeds and hyperparameters. In the updated version of the paper, we have softened the claim slightly. We also provided additional evidence for our observations (see below). It seems to us that a more detailed investigation in this direction might be a good area for future research.

> Is there any experiment demonstrating and comparing the effectiveness of policy constraints on the proposed dataset?

Although we did not initially planned a separate experiment, since we think the probability of improvement indicates it quite clearly, we added an additional table to the Appendix E summarizing the tuning of the alpha parameter responsible for the policy constraint for the CQL algorithm. As can be seen, when the impact of BC loss in CQL increases, the total reward also increases. Apart from the CQL algorithm, we observed similar behavior in all other algorithms except REM, since it does not have an explicit or implicit loss responsible for proximity to the behavioral policy.

References:
1. Emmons, S., Eysenbach, B., Kostrikov, I., & Levine, S. (2021). Rvs: What is essential for offline rl via supervised learning?
2. Kumar, A., Hong, J., Singh, A., & Levine, S. (2022). When should we prefer offline reinforcement learning over behavioral cloning?
3. Agarwal, R., Schwarzer, M., Castro, P. S., Courville, A. C., & Bellemare, M. (2021). Deep reinforcement learning at the edge of the statistical precipice

We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and concerns.

> Can you please clarify to what extent your library provides more than the combination of the individual existing parts?
> 

Although we utilize an existing dataset, our library offers a unique set of tools to aid researchers in tackling the Nethack environment with minimal effort and to test their ideas on a smaller scale with fast iterations.

As we state in our paper, we provide user-friendly interfaces (as recognized in the review) to facilitate working with the datasets. Also, we offer simple and straightforward baseline implementations along with fully open and accessible logs and configurations for all experiments on Wandb, enabling anyone to ensure reproducibility. As the result, the researchers can concentrate on validating their idea instead of having to implement and train baselines from scratch.

Additionally, we present a preliminary analysis of the results as well as an example of utilizing best practices from Agarwal et al., 2021 to report results using metrics that are more robust to noise than simple sample averages. Based on this, we propose potential future research directions that could greatly contribute to the improvement of the results. These are all distinct contributions that prior Nethack publications do not offer, and we believe they will be valuable to the offline RL community.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces Katakomba, an open-sourced benchmark for data-driven RL research on the NetHack environment. Katakomba aims to address three major obstacles that hinder the adoption of a large-scale NetHack dataset in offline RL research: implementation-wise, resource-wise, and benchmark-wise. It provides a fine-grained set of tasks that enable faster experimentation, clean implementations of several baseline offline RL methods, evaluation guidelines tailored for NetHack, and full training logs and configurations. Putting it together, Katakomba lowers the barrier to conducting data-driven RL research on NetHack.

strengths.value:
* This paper identifies the current challenges in adopting the large-scale NetHack dataset in offline RL research, and makes engineering efforts to address them. It perfectly fits the theme of Dataset & Benchmark track.
* The authors make significant contributions in making the large-scale NetHack dataset more readily adoptable, including compiling a new set of smaller datasets, creating more proper and faster data-loading pipelines, implementing several offline RL baselines, and evaluating those methods on data-driven NetHack tasks.
* NetHack is a challenging game that requires strong generalization abilities and extraordinary memory capacity, serving as a good testbed for building intelligent agents. The proposed benchmark will help promote research on data-driven NetHack and be of great practical value to the RL community.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: It is not clear how the normalized score (e.g., in Figure 1) is computed. Maybe I missed something. Shouldn't the normalized score lie within [0, 1]?

limitations.value: The limitations are well discussed in Section 6.

correctness.value: The designs are well-motivated and the experiments are well-executed.

clarity.value:
The paper is clearly written. I only have one minor suggestion:
* The 3 obstacles mentioned in the abstract are not consistent with those mentioned in Section 2. In the abstract one of them is tool-wise, but in Section 2 it becomes resource-wise.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper presents a set of tools for offline reinforcement learning (ORL) in the game NetHack. The paper diagnoses limitations of current tools for working with NetHack data and proposes changes to: (1) increase data loader speed, (2) provide standard ORL algorithm implementations with (LSTM) memory, and (3) use RLiable tools for benchmarking metrics (with metrics stored in Weights & Biases). The dataset is also subdivided into variants based on human expectations of difficulty, creating multiple levels task difficulty. Evaluations show that common ORL algorithms all perform equally (poorly) on the tasks, with none differing from vanilla behavior cloning (except REM, which fails to learn at all).

strengths.value:
# significance

Modest. Provides a new set of tooling around existing datasets. The tooling and best practices they support around benchmarking are welcome additions, particularly given the clear difficulty of the task for existing RL algorithms. Tooling has incremental value to accelerate research on this task and others could contribute more data to use with these tools.

# relevance

Modest. The ORL community is primarily interested in robotics at this time. NetHack has appeal as a task for game playing AI and so will appeal to that group. The limited success of RL in NetHack domain makes this a promising addition to help accelerate work in the game playing subfield. That said, the intersection of ORL and NetHack narrows the audience compared to alternative multi-task benchmarks of problems with large existing research communities.


# quality

Good. The empirical evaluations support two key points:
1) The new data loader can be much faster than the previous data loader. (Even with data modified to the standard RL form)
2) Baseline implementations of ORL algorithms do poorly on these tasks.


# ethical and social implications

Good. Nothing stands out. The dataset is for a video game with few direct real-world parallels and gathered from bots. The tooling simplifies interaction with this data, so there are no obvious novel social or ethical implications.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
# significance

I was unable to install the environment, so it would help to see some comments addressing those issues.

Considering ways to broaden the capabilities being offered:
- Can this benchmark be integrated with other existing ORL benchmarks? 
- Are there other games like NetHack that could be served through the same interface (testing forms of generalization)?
- How difficult might it be to gather new datasets using this tooling (with augmentations)?


# relevance

The paper would benefit from some reference to other audiences outside the NetHack community that may benefit from testing with this benchmark. The mention of "part of the ORL community studying discrete control, memory, and adaptivity" would benefit from some concrete examples.

Are there ways to show that interfacing to this benchmark would be the same (or identical?) to using D4RL or a related widely adopted standard?


# quality

Consider adding some experiments around computational scalability. What happens when more compute is available? What are the main bottlenecks (GPU? CPU? RAM?)? How much faster can training go and how does this compare to the AutoAscend dataset?


# ethical and social implications

Nothing.

limitations.value:
The limitations discuss weaknesses of the existing ORL implementations as they fail to achieve much success on the task. It would help to consider other limitations of the tooling itself:
- How well can the tooling support scaling to more compute?
- What can the tooling do to support gathering new datasets and sharing them?
- Are there opportunities to provide tools and training for sub-tasks? For example, completing certain in-game objectives or pre-training a state encoder.


The authors note no substantial negative societal implications of the work. This makes sense for providing better tooling to use datasets derived from bots playing a video game with only vague parallels to real life activities.

correctness.value:
Yes. The evaluations demonstrate that the task is hard for existing algorithms. The training shows progress, so the tools seem to be providing data correctly to train, even if the algorithms are failing to extract useful signal from that information.

The data loader experiments also support the claim of improving compared to the existing tools.

clarity.value: Yes. The analysis of weaknesses of the existing frameworks leads nicely into the proposed changes. Overall the text flows well and the key details are covered around experiment design and results.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Yes. This work focuses on tooling to improve data loading efficiency (with different trade-offs), along with simplified workflows that are more like typical tooling used for ORL. It would help to distinguish the tools here with D4RL, specifically to explain why D4RL cannot be adapted to this case.

documentation.value:
The dataset original sources are credited and the datasets are being hosted on HuggingFace, providing a stable location and maintenance provider (at least as stable as is generally available now). Responsible use concerns are minimal as the data was gathered using scripted bot gameplay.

The text references ongoing efforts to improve the tools to transition to the online learning case.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

- [Q0] How does the training time scale with different hardware configurations? How does this compare to the distributed Hambro et al. implementation?
- [Q1] Why normalize the scores if the bot is far from ideal behavior?
- [Q2] Are there reasonable hand-defined metrics to use instead for different levels of success?
	- Perhaps human benchmarks could define a reasonable score target. Possibly per task. Given the long lived NetHack community I would guess there's some standards for levels of success that could be adopted for benchmark standards.

title.value: Katakomba: Tools and Benchmarks for Data-Driven NetHack

abstract.value: NetHack is known as the frontier of reinforcement learning research where learning-based methods still need to catch up to rule-based solutions. One of the promising directions for a breakthrough is using pre-collected datasets similar to recent developments in robotics, recommender systems, and more under the umbrella of offline reinforcement learning (ORL). Recently, a large-scale NetHack dataset was released; while it was a necessary step forward, it has yet to gain wide adoption in the ORL community. In this work, we argue that there are three major obstacles for adoption: tool-wise, implementation-wise, and benchmark-wise. To address them, we develop an open-source library that provides workflow fundamentals familiar to the ORL community: pre-defined D4RL-style tasks, uncluttered baseline implementations, and reliable evaluation tools with accompanying configs and logs synced to the cloud.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
